::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- write code in a **script** with comments, and run it line by line;
- create **objects** with `<-` and give them good names;
- call **functions** using positional and named **arguments**;
- find help with `?`, `help()`, `example()` and vignettes, and **read error messages**;
- organise your work in an **RStudio Project** and build file paths with `here::here()` instead of `setwd()`.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
# Base R only. We use here::here() once, with the package::function() style.
```

## 1. Why do we need good habits from day one?

Two students analyse the same data. Student A types commands directly into the Console until the plot "looks right", then closes RStudio. Student B writes each step into a file, with a short comment explaining why. A month later the supervisor asks for the same plot with one penguin species removed.

Student A has to rediscover everything from scratch. Student B changes one line and re-runs the file.

This lesson is about becoming Student B. None of it is difficult, but these habits — scripts, clear names, projects, relative paths — save you hours every week.

## 2. Console vs scripts

You can type code in two places:

| | **Console** | **Script** (`.R` file in the Source pane) |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | Each line runs immediately | Nothing runs until you send it to the Console |
| Is it saved? | No (only in History, messily) | Yes — it is a text file |
| Use it for | Quick checks: `nrow(penguins)`, `?mean` | **Everything you want to keep** |

Create a script with *File → New File → R Script* (or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + N). Run the current line, or a selected block, with **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd + Enter** (macOS). Save it with a meaningful name, such as `penguin-summary.R`.

### Comments

Anything after `#` on a line is a **comment**: R ignores it. Comments are for humans — including you in three months.

```{r}
#| label: comments
# Average body mass of all penguins, in grams
mean(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)  # na.rm = TRUE skips missing values
```

Good comments explain **why**, not *what*. `# take the mean` above `mean(x)` adds nothing; `# use the median because body mass is skewed` adds a lot.

## 3. Objects and assignment

R stores results in **objects**. You create an object by **assigning** a value to a name with the arrow `<-` (read it as "gets"):

```{r}
#| label: assign
n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_penguins
```

The first line computes `nrow(penguins)` and stores the result under the name `n_penguins`; nothing is printed. The second line just types the name, and R prints its value. The object now appears in the *Environment* pane.

Objects can be reused and combined:

```{r}
#| label: reuse
n_species <- 3
n_penguins / n_species     # average number of penguins per species
```

And they can be **overwritten** without warning:

```{r}
#| label: overwrite
x <- 10
x <- x + 5    # take the old value of x, add 5, store it back in x
x
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `<-` or `=`?

`x = 10` also works at the top level, but the R community uses `<-` for assignment and keeps `=` for naming arguments inside function calls (Section 4). Following this convention makes code easier to read. In RStudio, **Alt + -** (Windows/Linux) or **Option + -** (macOS) types `<-` with spaces around it.
:::

### Naming rules

A name must start with a letter (or a dot not followed by a number) and can contain letters, numbers, `.` and `_`. R is **case-sensitive**: `Mass`, `mass` and `MASS` are three different objects.

| Name | Valid? | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| `body_mass_kg` | ✓ | Recommended style: `snake_case`, descriptive |
| `bodyMassKg` | ✓ | Valid, but not the tidyverse style |
| `x2` | ✓ | Fine for a quick calculation, poor for anything you keep |
| `2x` | ✗ | Cannot start with a number |
| `body mass` | ✗ | No spaces |
| `mean` | ✓ but avoid | Valid, but confusing: `mean()` is already a built-in function |

Avoid also `T`, `F`, `c`, `data` and `df` as names: they are already functions or constants in R.

## 4. Calling functions

A **function** takes inputs (called **arguments**), does something, and returns an output. You call it by writing its name followed by parentheses:

```{r}
#| label: fun-call
round(3.14159)
```

Most functions have several arguments. Look at `round()`: it has an argument `x` (the number) and an argument `digits` (how many decimals, default `0`). You can supply arguments in two ways:

```{r}
#| label: fun-args
round(3.14159, 2)                # positional: matched by order
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)   # named: matched by name
round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)   # named arguments can come in any order
```

All three lines give the same result. A common and readable compromise: give the **first one or two** arguments by position, and **name all the others**.

```{r}
#| label: seq-named
seq(1, 20, by = 3)
```

Arguments that have a **default value** can be omitted. To see the arguments and their defaults, use `args()` or the help page:

```{r}
#| label: args
args(round)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

`function (x, digits = 0, ...)` means: `round()` takes an argument `x` with **no default** (so you must provide it) and `digits` with default `0`. The `...` ("dots") means the function can accept further arguments that it passes on to other methods. Ignore the `NULL` on the last line: it is just what `args()` returns after printing.
:::

Functions can be **nested**: the inner one is evaluated first.

```{r}
#| label: nested
round(mean(penguins$flipper_len, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

Read it from the inside out: compute the mean flipper length (skipping missing values), then round it to one decimal. In [Lesson 9](../02-data/09-dplyr-verbs.qmd) you will meet the **pipe** `|>`, which lets you write the same thing left to right:

```{r}
#| label: pipe-teaser
penguins$flipper_len |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) |> round(1)
```

## 5. Getting help

Nobody remembers every function. Knowing how to find help is a core skill.

| You want… | Type |
|---|---|
| The help page of a function you know | `?mean` or `help("mean")` |
| To run the examples at the bottom of a help page | `example(mean)` |
| To search help pages for a word | `??regression` or `help.search("regression")` |
| Long-form tutorials that come with a package | `vignette(package = "dplyr")`, then `vignette("dplyr", package = "dplyr")` |
| To see which arguments a function takes | `args(fun)`, or press **Tab** after `fun(` in RStudio |

Every help page has the same sections. Read them in this order: **Description** (what it does), **Usage** (how to call it), **Arguments** (what each input means), **Value** (what it returns), and **Examples** (code you can copy). The examples are often the fastest way to understand a function.

### Reading error messages

Errors are normal: experienced programmers see dozens a day. The trick is to **read** them instead of panicking. R distinguishes three kinds of feedback:

| Kind | Starts with | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Error** | `Error` | R stopped; nothing was computed. |
| **Warning** | `Warning` | R computed something, but suspects a problem. **Check the result.** |
| **Message** | (anything else) | Just information. |

```{r}
#| label: error-examples
#| warning: true
#| error: true
sqrt("16")
log(-1)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `sqrt("16")` produces an **error**: `non-numeric argument to mathematical function`. The quotes make `"16"` a piece of text, not a number. Fix: `sqrt(16)`.
- `log(-1)` produces a **warning** (`NaNs produced`) and returns `NaN` ("not a number"): the logarithm of a negative number is undefined. R did not stop, but the result is not usable.
:::

When you get an error, a good routine is:

1. Read the message, slowly. It often says exactly what is wrong (`object 'peguins' not found` → typo).
2. Check spelling, capital letters, commas, matching parentheses and quotes.
3. Run the line piece by piece (the innermost function first).
4. Copy the error message into a search engine, *without* your own object names.

### Asking a good question

If you are still stuck, ask a teacher, a classmate or a forum such as the [Posit Community](https://forum.posit.co). A good question contains a **reprex** — a *minimal reproducible example*: the smallest piece of code that anyone can copy, paste and run to see your problem. It uses built-in data (or a few lines of made-up data), loads the needed packages, and shows the error. The `reprex` package can format such an example for you. Very often, while building the reprex, you find the bug yourself.

## 6. Projects and the working directory

Every R session has a **working directory**: the folder where R looks for files when you give it a file name without a full path. You can see it with:

```{r}
#| label: getwd
#| eval: false
getwd()
```

### RStudio Projects

An **RStudio Project** is a folder that contains everything for one analysis (data, scripts, reports) plus a small `.Rproj` file. Create one with *File → New Project → New Directory*. When you open a project (double-click the `.Rproj` file), RStudio automatically sets the working directory to that folder and starts a fresh R session. Positron offers the same idea through *File → Open Folder*.

A typical project layout:

```
penguin-analysis/
├── penguin-analysis.Rproj
├── data/
│   └── penguins_2025.csv
├── R/
│   └── clean-data.R
└── report.qmd
```

### Why never `setwd()`?

You will see old code starting with a line like `setwd("C:/Users/maria/Desktop/thesis")`. **Do not do this.** That path exists only on Maria's computer: on anyone else's machine (including Maria's new laptop) the script fails on line 1. Use a project instead, and refer to files with paths **relative** to the project folder.

The `here` package makes relative paths robust: `here::here()` always starts from the project root, no matter which sub-folder your script or Quarto document lives in.

```{r}
#| label: here-example
#| eval: false
here::here()                                # the project root folder
here::here("data", "penguins_2025.csv")     # .../penguin-analysis/data/penguins_2025.csv
penguins_new <- read.csv(here::here("data", "penguins_2025.csv"))
```

These lines are not run here because the file does not exist on this website; try them inside your own project.

## 7. Quarto documents in five lines

A **Quarto document** (`.qmd`) mixes text and code. When you *render* it (the **Render** button), Quarto runs the code and produces a report — HTML, PDF or Word — with the results inserted. A minimal example:

````markdown
---
title: "Penguin report"
---

Penguins weigh, on average:

```{{r}}
mean(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```
````

The part between `---` lines is the **header** (YAML). The block that starts with ```` ```{r} ```` is a **code chunk**: R code that is run when the document is rendered, with its output placed right below. Everything else is ordinary text. This whole course is written this way.

## 8. `renv` in two sentences

Packages change over time, so code that works today may behave differently after an update. The `renv` package records the exact package versions a project uses in a file called `renv.lock`, so that you (or a colleague) can restore the same versions later with `renv::restore()`.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Working only in the Console.** Anything not in a script is lost when you close R. Write scripts from the start.
2. **`x < - 5` instead of `x <- 5`.** With a space in the middle, R reads "is `x` less than minus 5?" (and fails if `x` does not exist). Keep `<-` together.
3. **Capital letters and typos.** `Mean(x)` or `penguins$Body_mass` fail or return `NULL`: R is case-sensitive.
4. **Ignoring warnings.** A warning means R produced a result it does not trust. Check it before moving on.
5. **`setwd()` with an absolute path.** It breaks on every other computer. Use an RStudio Project and `here::here()`.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What is printed by `y <- 3 * 4`?

Nothing. An assignment stores the value (12) in `y` silently. Type `y` (or wrap the assignment in parentheses, `(y <- 3 * 4)`) to print it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Are `round(2.567, 1)` and `round(digits = 1, 2.567)` the same?

Yes. Named arguments are matched first (`digits = 1`); the remaining unnamed value is then matched by position to the first unused argument, `x`. Both return 2.6. The second form is legal but harder to read.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A classmate's script begins with `setwd("/Users/luca/Documents/R")`. What do you suggest?

Delete that line, put the script and data inside an RStudio Project, and build file paths with `here::here("data", "file.csv")`. The code will then run unchanged on any computer.
:::

## 10. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — objects.** A penguin weighs 4,250 g. Store this value in an object called `mass_g`, then create `mass_kg` by dividing by 1000, and print `mass_kg`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_02_1
mass_g <- ______
mass_kg <- ______ / 1000
mass_kg
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_02_1"}
Assignment is `name <- value`. In the second line, divide the object `mass_g`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_02_1"}
```r
mass_g <- 4250
mass_kg <- mass_g / 1000
mass_kg
```
The result is 4.25. Notice that `mass_kg` is computed from `mass_g`: if you change the first line, re-running the script updates everything.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — named arguments.** (a) Use `seq()` to create the numbers from 0 to 100 in steps of 25, naming the `by` argument. (b) Use `seq()` again to create **exactly 5** equally spaced numbers between 0 and 1 (look at the `length.out` argument). (c) Round `pi` to 3 decimals using a named argument.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_02_2
seq(0, 100, ______ = 25)
seq(0, 1, ______ = 5)
round(pi, ______ = 3)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_02_2"}
The argument names are `by`, `length.out` and `digits`. Run `args(seq.default)` to see them all.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_02_2"}
```r
seq(0, 100, by = 25)        # 0 25 50 75 100
seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)   # 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00
round(pi, digits = 3)       # 3.142
```
Naming `by` and `length.out` matters: `seq(0, 1, 5)` would be read as `by = 5` and return just `0`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug.** Each line below contains one mistake. Run the code, read the error message, and fix each line so that it runs.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_02_3
mean_mass <- mean(penguins$body_weight, na.rm = TRUE)
Mean_mass
round(mean_mass digits = 0)
sqrt("25")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_02_3"}
Run one line at a time. Look for: a wrong column name (run `names(penguins)` to see the real ones), a capital letter, a missing comma, and text where a number is needed.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_02_3"}
```r
mean_mass <- mean(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_mass
round(mean_mass, digits = 0)
sqrt(25)
```
The first bug is the sneakiest: there is no column `body_weight`, so `penguins$body_weight` returns `NULL` and `mean()` returns `NA` with a *warning* (`argument is not numeric or logical`), not an error. Always read warnings.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — arguments and examples.** (a) Use `args()` to find the arguments of `median()` and the default value of `na.rm`. (b) Run the examples from its help page with `example()`. (c) Use what you learned to compute the median of `c(1, NA, 3)`. (Help pages themselves open best in RStudio or Positron: on your own computer, also try `?median`.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_02_4
args(______)
example(______)
median(c(1, NA, 3), ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_02_4"}
Both `args()` and `example()` take the function name, e.g. `example(median)`. The missing argument in (c) is `na.rm = TRUE`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_02_4"}
```r
args(median)                       # function (x, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
example(median)
median(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE)  # 2
```
`na.rm` is a logical value: if `TRUE`, missing values are removed before computing the median. Its default is `FALSE`, so `median(c(1, NA, 3))` returns `NA`.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — your first project.** (a) Create a new RStudio Project called `r-course`. (b) Inside it, create a folder `data` and a script `first-script.R`. (c) In the script, write (with comments) code that prints the number of rows of `penguins` and the mean bill length, then save it. (d) Close RStudio, reopen the project by double-clicking `r-course.Rproj`, and run `here::here("data")`. What does it print?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
# first-script.R — first look at the penguins data
nrow(penguins)                               # number of penguins
mean(penguins$bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)        # mean bill length (mm)

here::here("data")   # full path to <your project>/data
```
`here::here("data")` prints the full path of the `data` folder inside your project. If you move the project to another computer, the printed path changes, but your code does not need to.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 6 — a five-line Quarto report.** In your project, create *File → New File → Quarto Document*, delete the template content and write a short report with a title, one sentence and one chunk that computes the median flipper length of the penguins. Render it to HTML.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
````markdown
---
title: "My first report"
---

The median flipper length (mm) of the penguins is:

```{{r}}
median(penguins$flipper_len, na.rm = TRUE)
```
````
Click **Render**. If it fails, read the error in the *Background Jobs* / *Render* pane: the line number points to the problem.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#` | Starts a comment |
| `name <- value` | Creates (or overwrites) an object |
| `fun(arg1, name = value)` | Calls a function with positional and named arguments |
| `args(fun)` | Shows the arguments and defaults of a function |
| `?fun`, `help()`, `example()`, `vignette()` | Getting help |
| Error / Warning / Message | Stopped / suspicious result / information |
| RStudio Project, `here::here()` | Self-contained folder and robust relative paths |
| Quarto (`.qmd`) | Text + code chunks rendered into a report |
| `renv` | Records package versions for a project |

- Keep **everything** you care about in scripts, not in the Console.
- Use descriptive `snake_case` names and `<-` for assignment.
- Name the arguments that are not obvious.
- Read error **and warning** messages; build a reprex when you ask for help.
- Never `setwd()`: use Projects and `here::here()`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
